# Implementation ## Workspace layout cyspbot is a pnpm workspace with three deployable Cloudflare Workers: - `workers/cyspbot` publishes `@cyspbot/cyspbot` and Worker `cyspbot`. - `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-receiver` publishes `@cyspbot/github-webhook-receiver` and Worker `cyspbot-github-webhook-receiver`. - `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-processor` publishes `@cyspbot/github-webhook-processor` and Worker `cyspbot-github-webhook-processor`. Shared packages: - `packages/http` provides bounded body reading, request-body handling, JSON responses, and problem-details responses. - `packages/token-exchange` provides the internal RFC 8693 Token Exchange Client. - `packages/github-webhook-jobs` provides the versioned job contract shared by the webhook receiver and processor. The root `wrangler.jsonc` points at `test/support/root-test-harness.ts`. It supplies common bindings to unit tests and is not a deployable product Worker. ## Root Worker flow `workers/cyspbot/src/worker.ts` dispatches exactly `/token` to the private `src/token-proxy.ts` forwarding module and handles the root page and fallback responses directly. Endpoint configuration is read inside forwarding, keeping root and fallback handling independent. See the [service contract](service-contract.md#routes) for route and response behavior. In production, this Worker is the Custom Domain origin for `/` and `/token`. The more specific webhook route still selects the independently deployed receiver. The root page and forwarding handler share source and deployment ownership, so one Worker avoids an extra publication target and token route. They also share a credential-bearing runtime; `SECURITY.md` defines that accepted trust boundary. ## Webhook Worker flow `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-receiver/src/worker.ts` exposes only `POST /github/webhooks`. It rejects unknown routes and other methods before calling `handleGitHubWebhookRequest`. `handleGitHubWebhookRequest` owns the HTTP response and privately authenticates the envelope. It: 1. resolves `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` from a direct Worker secret or Secrets Store binding through its private secret adapter; 2. requires `application/json` and reads at most `256 KiB`; 3. requires the event, delivery, signature, and installation-target headers; 4. requires the target type `integration` and the configured `GITHUB_APP_ID`; 5. verifies the exact bytes and decoded signature with Web Crypto HMAC-SHA256 verification; 6. decodes the authenticated body as UTF-8 with fatal error handling and parses it as JSON; 7. classifies `issue_comment` deliveries with `action: "created"` and a trimmed comment body exactly equal to `/cyspbot status`; 8. sends the derived version-1 job to `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_JOBS` and waits for the queue write; and 9. returns the acknowledgement shape for ping, matching, or other events. The receiver sends only a derived job to the queue, using the same job parser as the processor to validate the projected job before publication. The [service contract](service-contract.md#webhook-responses) defines the job fields and HTTP responses. ## Webhook processor flow `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-processor` consumes `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs`. It validates each versioned job with the shared parser, then delegates token acquisition and reaction creation to its private `src/github/reactions.ts` module. The module follows redirects manually to preserve the reaction POST: [automatic Fetch redirects](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-redirect-fetch) can turn a `301` or `302` POST into a GET. Intermediate response bodies are cancelled without awaiting cleanup. The [service contract](service-contract.md#webhook-responses) defines redirect limits, acknowledgement, retries, and diagnostic handling. ## Runtime bindings - The cyspbot Worker's `TOKEN_PROXY_ENDPOINT`: non-secret Worker variable containing the canonical HTTPS broker App endpoint URL. - The cyspbot Worker's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER`: required HTTP Service Binding to the broker's default handler. The binding selects the service; the endpoint URL selects the App path. - `GITHUB_APP_ID`: required non-secret variable used to bind deliveries to the intended GitHub App. - `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`: required Worker secret or Cloudflare Secrets Store binding. - `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_JOBS`: Queue producer binding used by the webhook receiver for derived status-reaction jobs. - `cyspbot-github-webhook-processor` consumes `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs` and sends exhausted jobs to `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq`. - The processor's `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_ISSUER`: RPC Service Binding to a separately deployed `WorkloadIdentityIssuer` entrypoint. Its `issueToken(audience)` operation returns an `IssuedToken`; the issuer deployment owns the workload subject and signing details. This RPC is a workload-identity interface, not an OAuth token endpoint. - The processor's `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN_AUDIENCE`: non-secret Worker variable containing the logical audience requested from the issuer and accepted by the broker. - The processor's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER`: Service Binding used by the OAuth Client to call the broker's existing RFC 8693 Token Endpoint with `fetch`. - The processor's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER_TOKEN_ENDPOINT`: non-secret Worker variable containing the broker's token endpoint URL. It is separate from the logical Workload Identity Token audience. ## Token Exchange Client The internal Token Exchange Client in `packages/token-exchange` first calls the issuer RPC, then posts the returned short-lived Workload Identity Token as a workload identity assertion to the configured broker endpoint as the RFC 8693 `subject_token` under the broker's OIDC ID Token subject-token profile. It requests a GitHub App Installation Access Token with a canonical GitHub `resource` and explicit permission `scope`; the broker remains the source of truth for normalization, OIDC ID Token profile verification, and Token Issuance Policy. On success, the client returns a `GitHubAppInstallationAccessToken`. It accepts the case-insensitive `Bearer` token type and uses the requested scope when the broker omits an unchanged scope, following [RFC 8693 section 2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.2.1). An explicit scope must be a non-empty string and is returned as issued. The client's GitHub installation-token profile requires a non-empty `access_token`, `issued_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token`, and a positive integer `expires_in`. RFC 8693 defines `expires_in` as recommended. On an OAuth failure, the client throws a `GitHubAppTokenBrokerError` containing the HTTP status and OAuth error code and description. Credential logging restrictions are defined in the [security boundary](../SECURITY.md#security-boundary). The client is an internal library operation and is not exposed as an HTTP route. Production service names, binding resource identifiers, secret-store references, and Cloudflare Workload Identity properties belong to the separate deployment repository. Terraform manages production queues, their consumer, domains, and routes; see [deployment ownership](deployment.md#separate-deployment-pipeline). The public Worker Wrangler files contain only local-development and dry-run service targets and values. ## Tests and validation Tests live in each owning package or Worker’s `test/` directory alongside `src/`. Worker integration tests and their fixtures live under `test/integration/`; helpers shared by tests within a Worker live under its `test/support/`. The root `test/` contains the shared unit harness, its own test, and integration tests spanning multiple Workers. Tests use local source imports for internal seams and package imports for package interfaces and dependencies. Worker package exports expose only their entrypoints. The root `vitest.config.ts` selects the unit suite, three Worker integration suites, and the built-Worker integration suite, and owns combined coverage. Production TypeScript checks and the Node-import lint restriction apply to `src/`; the root test TypeScript configuration also covers package-local tests and their helpers. CI retains separate validation workflows. New commits cancel superseded CI runs for the same pull request. Every main push keeps its own CI run so successful checks can trigger the deployment update. The workspace's 72-hour minimum release age applies to local dependency resolution and the daily transitive updater, matching Dependabot's release-age floor. The unit and individual Worker integration suites run in Workerd through `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` with Vitest 5. Keep Vitest and its V8 coverage provider on matching versions supported by the published Cloudflare plugin. Vite is an explicit development dependency because Vitest 5 requires it as a peer. The explicit `peer-dependencies:check` gate enforces peer compatibility after resolution; [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md) owns the dependency-update policy. Dependabot groups the Cloudflare test plugin, Wrangler, and Workers types together. Vitest and its coverage provider form a separate group; Vite remains separate. Node declarations stay on Node 24, with major updates reserved for a runtime upgrade. Strict peer validation checks compatibility across these groups. Each Vitest project prohibits focused tests. Each Worker's production TypeScript check uses the runtime types generated from its Wrangler compatibility date and flags. Coverage uses native V8 collection in Node and plugin-managed Workerd, avoiding source coverage instrumentation. The Cloudflare plugin configures inspector compatibility settings for its test runtime. Reports use Istanbul's coverage model and retain the text and LCOV reporters and Codecov upload. Coverage explicitly includes package and Worker source files, including unimported files, and excludes type declarations. No numerical coverage thresholds are configured. V8 has [documented measurement limitations](https://github.com/AriPerkkio/ast-v8-to-istanbul#limitations): unexecuted default arguments and statements after a throwing call can appear covered. Assert defaults and failure-path behavior directly; percentages alone do not prove execution. When changing providers, compare source inventories and uncovered locations as well as totals. The unit project exercises the root response, bounded body reading, request-body size and status handling, signature/target validation through HTTP responses, queue-job classification and processing, token-exchange response mapping, and all Worker factories. Separate Workerd integration projects load each Worker's real Wrangler configuration and entrypoint. The processor integration project loads the processor Wrangler configuration, runs a local `WorkloadIdentityIssuer` named-entrypoint fixture through a Workerd Service Binding, and exercises the queue entrypoint's token exchange. The test checks the broker request, exact GitHub token use, and queue acknowledgement or retry through Cloudflare message-batch helpers. This validates the local RPC serialization and method contract; it does not test the separately deployed issuer implementation. The unit project uses structural fixtures for validation failures. The `built-workers-integration` project runs in Node and uses Wrangler's `createTestHarness()` to build and run all three Workers with their production compatibility dates and flags. It checks the root page, bodyless responses for HEAD, unsupported methods and unknown paths, and rejection of matching webhooks with an invalid signature or installation target. It sends signed Webhook Deliveries through the receiver's configured queue to the processor and exercises GitHub's success responses for both new and existing reactions. Local issuer and broker fixtures validate the token exchange; a Node `fetch` mock validates the GitHub reaction request and blocks other outbound requests. The queue connection uses the source Wrangler configurations for local testing. This suite complements the individual processor tests that assert acknowledgement and retry behavior. The separately launched built Workers run outside Vitest's coverage collection. Vitest's async-leak diagnostics use Node's `async_hooks`; Workerd does not implement the hooks used by this detector. To investigate leaked resources in the Node test harness, run: ```bash node --run test -- --project built-workers-integration --detectAsyncLeaks ``` This diagnoses resources in the Node test process; it does not detect leaks inside the Workers. Keep this slower diagnostic mode opt-in. Choose required checks using [Contributing: Validation scope](../CONTRIBUTING.md#validation-scope). `vitest.config.ts` owns the test projects and fixtures; `package.json` owns the validation commands. Keep fixture-backed local integration results distinct from verification of separately deployed services. ## Token Endpoint forwarding The private `workers/cyspbot/src/token-proxy.ts` module owns the [Token Endpoint forwarding contract](service-contract.md#token-endpoint-proxy) using `env.GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER.fetch` with a fixed canonical HTTPS URL and manual redirect handling. It never falls back to global fetch. The webhook processor retains its separate broker binding and endpoint variable. Workerd integration tests exercise the HTTP Service Binding, and built-Worker tests route requests to a local broker Worker fixture while rejecting public fetches. They check canonical App selection, request bytes, preserved admission headers, and redirect rejection. They establish transport behavior, not the origin or authenticity of an edge identity. Production ingress and spoofing checks remain required; see `SECURITY.md` for the deployment trust requirements. # Service contract This document is authoritative for the observable behavior implemented by cyspbot. ## Routes | Route | Method | Purpose | Success | | ------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | | `/` | `GET` | Identify cyspbot as a bot | `200` HTML | | `/token` | Any | Forward to the deployment-configured broker Token Endpoint | Broker response | | `/github/webhooks` | `POST` | Authenticate, classify, and queue GitHub App webhook jobs | `202` JSON | `HEAD /` returns the same status and headers as `GET /` without a response body. Other methods at `/` return an empty `405` response with `Allow: GET, HEAD`. The cyspbot Worker handles exactly `/token` as described below and returns an empty `404` response for every other path, regardless of method. More specific production Worker routes run before the root Worker and own the response within their route patterns. Unsupported methods on `/github/webhooks` return `405` problem details with `Allow: POST`. ## Root page The `/` response has media type `text/html; charset=utf-8` and is equivalent to the minimal document: ```html cyspbot

beep, boop. i am a bot.

``` ## Webhook request requirements The receiver requires: - a primary media type of `application/json` (parameters are allowed); - a body no larger than `256 KiB`; - `X-GitHub-Event`; - `X-GitHub-Delivery`; - `X-Hub-Signature-256` in GitHub's lowercase `sha256=<64 lowercase hex characters>` form; - `X-GitHub-Hook-Installation-Target-Type: integration`; - `X-GitHub-Hook-Installation-Target-ID` equal to `GITHUB_APP_ID`; and - a syntactically valid JSON body encoded as UTF-8. The signature is verified over the exact request bytes using `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. The body is parsed only after its target and signature authenticate. ## Webhook responses Accepted ping deliveries return: ```http HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted Content-Type: application/json {"accepted":true,"event":"ping"} ``` Other accepted events return: ```http HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted Content-Type: application/json {"accepted":true} ``` An authenticated `issue_comment` delivery creates a queue job only when its `action` is `created` and the trimmed comment body is exactly `/cyspbot status`. The job contains: ```json { "kind": "github.issue-comment.status-reaction", "version": 1, "deliveryId": "delivery-123", "repository": { "owner": "chikachow", "name": "cyspbot" }, "commentId": 42 } ``` The receiver waits for the queue write before returning `202`. Authenticated events that do not classify to this job receive `202` without a queue write. The receiver validates the derived job before publication: comment IDs must be positive safe integers, delivery IDs must be non-empty, and repository parts must be non-empty, at most 100 characters, and contain no path separators, query/fragment delimiters, or control characters. Repository parts must also be well-formed Unicode strings and cannot be `.` or `..`, so URL encoding neither throws nor changes the repository path. Payloads that cannot produce a valid job are acknowledged without a queue write. The receiver does not apply repository authorization filtering. A queue write failure returns `503 Service Unavailable`. GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed webhooks. Ingress is best effort until publication succeeds; operators manually redeliver failed deliveries after resolving the cause. See [delivery recovery](deployment.md#delivery-recovery). The processor requests a [GitHub App Installation Access Token](implementation.md#token-exchange-client) with `issues:write pull_requests:write` for the canonical GitHub Repository Resource and posts the `eyes` reaction to the comment. GitHub `200` and `201` responses complete the job. The processor follows at most three `301`, `302`, `307`, or `308` redirects, preserving the reaction POST, body, and authorization. Redirect destinations must remain on `https://api.github.com` without URL credentials. A supported redirect with an unparseable `Location` URL or a chain requiring more than three permitted redirects retries through the queue. Diagnostics record `redirectFailure` as `invalid_location` or `too_many_redirects`; the `Location` header is not logged. Missing `Location`, unsupported redirect statuses, and disallowed destinations stop the request without following the redirect; the job retries through the queue. Cancellation of unused response bodies is best effort and does not delay acknowledgement or cause a retry. Every failure while processing a valid job retries, including issuer failures, broker denials or malformed responses, GitHub HTTP errors, and network failures. Only GitHub `200` and `201` complete a valid job. Invalid queue jobs are acknowledged and rejected before requesting credentials. The queue uses one-message batches, five retries, a 60-second default retry delay, and the `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq` dead-letter queue. GitHub HTTP error responses honor numeric `Retry-After` and exhausted primary-quota `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers, using the longer wait with a 60-second minimum and Cloudflare's 24-hour maximum. Without a valid hint, GitHub HTTP error responses use exponential backoff starting at 60 seconds, capped at 24 hours. Transport, issuer, and broker failures use the queue's 60-second default. Cloudflare transfers jobs that exhaust the retry budget to the dead-letter queue for operator recovery; the processor does not acknowledge failed valid jobs or infer exhaustion from their attempt count. GitHub error-body diagnostics have a one-second total read budget and a 16 KiB size limit. On timeout the processor cancels the unfinished read, retains status and header diagnostics, and logs `bodyReadTimedOut: true`. Stream failures and size-limit failures retain header diagnostics and log `bodyReadFailed: true`. Error-body contents and read failures affect diagnostics, not whether the job retries. Available response headers still determine the retry delay. Rejections use RFC 9457-style problem-details JSON with `type`, `title`, and `status` fields: | Condition | Status | | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -----: | | Missing, empty, or unreadable webhook secret configuration | `500` | | Non-JSON media type | `415` | | Body exceeds `256 KiB` | `413` | | Missing event, delivery, or signature header | `400` | | Target type or target App ID mismatch | `401` | | Malformed or invalid signature | `401` | | Authenticated body is not UTF-8 JSON | `400` | | A matching job cannot be written to the queue | `503` | Repeated delivery IDs are accepted. Queue delivery is at least once, and the processor treats both successful GitHub reaction response statuses as completion, so repeated jobs do not require a separate deduplication store. ## Logging and retention Rejected deliveries may log the delivery ID, event, Cloudflare Ray ID, and response status. Raw request bodies, signature values, and webhook secrets are not logged or retained. Processor failures log the queue message ID, delivery ID (at most 128 characters), attempt count, status, and bounded GitHub diagnostics or a recognized OAuth error code. Unrecognized broker codes are logged as `unrecognized_error`; broker descriptions and credentials are excluded. ## Token Endpoint proxy The cyspbot Worker forwards exactly `/token` to the deployment-owned canonical `/github/apps/{app_slug}/token` HTTPS URL through the required `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER` HTTP Service Binding. This diagnoses resources in the Node test process; it does not detect leaks
inside the Workers. Keep this slower diagnostic mode opt-in.

Choose required checks using [Contributing: Validation scope](../CONTRIBUTING.md#validation-scope).
`vitest.config.ts` owns the test projects and fixtures; `package.json` owns
the validation commands. Keep fixture-backed local integration results distinct
from verification of separately deployed services.

## Token Endpoint forwarding

The private `workers/cyspbot/src/token-proxy.ts` module owns the
[Token Endpoint forwarding contract](service-contract.md#token-endpoint-proxy)
using `env.GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER.fetch` with a fixed canonical HTTPS URL and
manual redirect handling. It never falls back to global fetch. The webhook
processor retains its separate broker binding and endpoint variable.

Workerd integration tests exercise the HTTP Service Binding, and built-Worker
tests route requests to a local broker Worker fixture while rejecting public
fetches. They check canonical App selection, request bytes, preserved admission
headers, and redirect rejection. They establish transport behavior, not the
origin or authenticity of an edge identity. Production ingress and spoofing
checks remain required; see `SECURITY.md` for the deployment trust requirements.
# Service contract

This document is authoritative for the observable behavior implemented by cyspbot.

## Routes

| Route              | Method | Purpose                                                    | Success         |
| ------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| `/`                | `GET`  | Identify cyspbot as a bot                                  | `200` HTML      |
| `/token`           | Any    | Forward to the deployment-configured broker Token Endpoint | Broker response |
| `/github/webhooks` | `POST` | Authenticate, classify, and queue GitHub App webhook jobs  | `202` JSON      |

`HEAD /` returns the same status and headers as `GET /` without a response body. Other methods at `/` return an empty `405` response with `Allow: GET, HEAD`. The cyspbot Worker handles exactly `/token` as described below and returns an empty `404` response for every other path, regardless of method. More specific production Worker routes run before the root Worker and own the response within their route patterns. Unsupported methods on `/github/webhooks` return `405` problem details with `Allow: POST`.

## Root page

The `/` response has media type `text/html; charset=utf-8` and is equivalent to the minimal document:

```html
<!doctype html><title>cyspbot</title>
<p>beep, boop. i am a bot.</p>
```

## Webhook request requirements

The receiver requires:

- a primary media type of `application/json` (parameters are allowed);
- a body no larger than `256 KiB`;
- `X-GitHub-Event`;
- `X-GitHub-Delivery`;
- `X-Hub-Signature-256` in GitHub's lowercase `sha256=<64 lowercase hex characters>` form;
- `X-GitHub-Hook-Installation-Target-Type: integration`;
- `X-GitHub-Hook-Installation-Target-ID` equal to `GITHUB_APP_ID`; and
- a syntactically valid JSON body encoded as UTF-8.

The signature is verified over the exact request bytes using `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. The body is parsed only after its target and signature authenticate.

## Webhook responses

Accepted ping deliveries return:

```http
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json

{"accepted":true,"event":"ping"}
```

Other accepted events return:

```http
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json

{"accepted":true}
```

An authenticated `issue_comment` delivery creates a queue job only when its
`action` is `created` and the trimmed comment body is exactly
`/cyspbot status`. The job contains:

```json
{
  "kind": "github.issue-comment.status-reaction",
  "version": 1,
  "deliveryId": "delivery-123",
  "repository": {
    "owner": "chikachow",
    "name": "cyspbot"
  },
  "commentId": 42
}
```

The receiver waits for the queue write before returning `202`. Authenticated
events that do not classify to this job receive `202` without a queue write.
The receiver validates the derived job before publication: comment IDs must be positive safe integers, delivery IDs must be non-empty, and repository parts must be non-empty, at most 100 characters, and contain no path separators, query/fragment delimiters, or control characters. Repository parts must also be well-formed Unicode strings and cannot be `.` or `..`, so URL encoding neither throws nor changes the repository path. Payloads that cannot produce a valid job are acknowledged without a queue write. The receiver does not apply repository authorization filtering. A queue write failure
returns `503 Service Unavailable`. GitHub does not automatically redeliver
failed webhooks. Ingress is best effort until publication succeeds; operators
manually redeliver failed deliveries after resolving the cause. See
[delivery recovery](deployment.md#delivery-recovery).

The processor requests a [GitHub App Installation Access Token](implementation.md#token-exchange-client) with
`issues:write pull_requests:write` for the canonical GitHub Repository Resource and posts the
`eyes` reaction to the comment. GitHub `200` and `201` responses complete the
job. The processor follows at most three `301`, `302`, `307`, or `308` redirects,
preserving the reaction POST, body, and authorization. Redirect destinations must
remain on `https://api.github.com` without URL credentials. A supported redirect
with an unparseable `Location` URL or a chain requiring more than three permitted
redirects retries through the queue. Diagnostics record `redirectFailure` as
`invalid_location` or `too_many_redirects`; the `Location` header is not logged.
Missing `Location`, unsupported redirect statuses, and disallowed destinations
stop the request without following the redirect; the job retries through the queue.
Cancellation of unused response bodies is best effort and does not
delay acknowledgement or cause a retry. Every failure while processing a valid
job retries, including issuer failures, broker denials or malformed responses,
GitHub HTTP errors, and network failures. Only GitHub `200` and `201` complete
a valid job. Invalid queue jobs are acknowledged and rejected before requesting
credentials. The queue uses one-message batches, five
retries, a 60-second default retry delay, and the
`cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq` dead-letter queue. GitHub HTTP error responses honor numeric
`Retry-After` and exhausted primary-quota `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers, using
the longer wait with a 60-second minimum and Cloudflare's 24-hour maximum.
Without a valid hint, GitHub HTTP error responses use exponential backoff starting at
60 seconds, capped at 24 hours. Transport, issuer, and broker failures use the
queue's 60-second default. Cloudflare transfers jobs that exhaust the retry
budget to the dead-letter queue for operator recovery; the processor does not
acknowledge failed valid jobs or infer exhaustion from their attempt count.

GitHub error-body diagnostics have a one-second total read budget and a 16 KiB
size limit. On timeout the processor cancels the unfinished read, retains status
and header diagnostics, and logs `bodyReadTimedOut: true`. Stream failures and
size-limit failures retain header diagnostics and log `bodyReadFailed: true`.
Error-body contents and read failures affect diagnostics, not whether the job
retries. Available response headers still determine the retry delay.

Rejections use RFC 9457-style problem-details JSON with `type`, `title`, and `status` fields:

| Condition                                                  | Status |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | -----: |
| Missing, empty, or unreadable webhook secret configuration |  `500` |
| Non-JSON media type                                        |  `415` |
| Body exceeds `256 KiB`                                     |  `413` |
| Missing event, delivery, or signature header               |  `400` |
| Target type or target App ID mismatch                      |  `401` |
| Malformed or invalid signature                             |  `401` |
| Authenticated body is not UTF-8 JSON                       |  `400` |
| A matching job cannot be written to the queue              |  `503` |

Repeated delivery IDs are accepted. Queue delivery is at least once, and the
processor treats both successful GitHub reaction response statuses as
completion, so repeated jobs do not require a separate deduplication store.

## Logging and retention

Rejected deliveries may log the delivery ID, event, Cloudflare Ray ID, and response status. Raw request bodies, signature values, and webhook secrets are not logged or retained.

Processor failures log the queue message ID, delivery ID (at most 128 characters), attempt count, status, and bounded GitHub diagnostics or a recognized OAuth error code. Unrecognized broker codes are logged as `unrecognized_error`; broker descriptions and credentials are excluded.

## Token Endpoint proxy

The cyspbot Worker forwards exactly `/token` to the deployment-owned canonical
`/github/apps/{app_slug}/token` HTTPS URL through the required
`GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER` HTTP Service Binding.
It preserves the method and request bytes. The configured URL determines the
App path; the Service Binding selects the broker Worker. Both are deployment-owned,
and incoming query parameters cannot change them. Incoming `Host` is discarded. The proxy sets
`x-real-ip` from edge-supplied `CF-Connecting-IP`, or removes it if that header is
absent; other headers are forwarded subject to Cloudflare's subrequest behavior.
The incoming `CF-Connecting-IP` is retained. The broker uses it for admission,
not token authorization, and retains its shared `unknown` bucket when it is
absent. Public ingress must establish trustworthy identity; Service Binding
callers can supply these headers, as described in `SECURITY.md`.
It returns non-3xx broker response status, headers, and bytes unchanged,
including OAuth failures and admission responses. It does not cache responses,
follow or forward redirects, parse tokens, retry requests, or fall back to public fetch. The broker owns request limits,
OIDC verification, policy, GitHub I/O deadlines, and issuance observations.
Endpoint configuration and the binding are used only for `/token`; missing or invalid configuration does not affect the root page or unmatched paths, which make no outbound requests.
Every upstream 3xx response, invalid endpoint configuration, missing or unusable binding, or binding transport failure
before an upstream response is received returns `503` with
`{"error":"temporarily_unavailable"}`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, and
`Pragma: no-cache`; upstream redirect headers and bodies are discarded. `/token/` and other path variants remain unknown routes.
# Security Policy

## Reporting vulnerabilities

Please report security vulnerabilities privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting feature. Do not open a public issue containing exploit details, webhook secrets, payloads, or deployment credentials.

## Security boundary

cyspbot accepts GitHub App webhook deliveries. The important security properties are:

- request bodies are bounded to `256 KiB` before parsing;
- the delivery target must be the configured GitHub App ID;
- the exact request body must authenticate under `X-Hub-Signature-256` and the configured webhook secret;
- the authenticated body must be valid JSON before acknowledgement;
- raw webhook bodies, webhook secrets, workload identity assertions, and issued tokens are not logged or retained;
- only authenticated, newly created `/cyspbot status` comments produce a minimal versioned Status Reaction Job;
- the receiver awaits durable queue publication before acknowledging a matching command;
- only trusted producers may write to the queue, and the processor validates each job before requesting a token;
- the processor requests `issues:write pull_requests:write` for one repository and uses the issued token to add an `eyes` reaction; and
- the external broker owns workload identity verification and token issuance policy. Queue access and broker policy are deployment-owned trust controls.

The receiver does not filter repositories or comment authors. The broker must authorize the processor's workload identity and requested repository/permissions. Webhook target headers are routing metadata; authenticity depends on the body signature and a secret dedicated to the configured GitHub App. Repeated deliveries are allowed, and successful reaction creation or an existing reaction completes the job.

## Deployment secrets

Never commit deployment secrets, local `.dev.vars`, `.env`, webhook secrets, Cloudflare API tokens, or generated Wrangler state.

The webhook receiver needs:

- `GITHUB_APP_ID`, a non-secret Worker variable; and
- `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, supplied by a Worker secret or Cloudflare Secrets Store.

The cyspbot Worker serves both the root page and the Token Endpoint Proxy, so
its runtime is trusted with incoming identity tokens and outgoing access tokens.
Keep forwarding isolated from root-page handling; configuration failures affect
only `/token`. It forwards only to a deployment-owned canonical HTTPS
App URL through the required `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER` HTTP Service Binding,
without caching, retries, public-fetch fallback, or token logging. The binding
selects the broker Worker; the configured URL selects its App path. Both are
trusted deployment configuration. This binding targets the default HTTP handler,
not the GitHub App Information RPC or Workload Identity issuer. It does not grant
access to signing keys, the ability to mint workload assertions, or token issuance
authority. The broker authenticates the supplied subject token and applies its
App-specific Token Issuance Policy independently of transport.

The proxy rejects all upstream 3xx responses without forwarding their headers or
bodies, preventing those responses from directing clients to replay subject tokens
elsewhere. Incoming `Host` is discarded and incoming query parameters cannot
change the configured URL. The proxy preserves `CF-Connecting-IP`, sets
`x-real-ip` from it, and removes `x-real-ip` when that identity is absent. Public
ingress must replace client-supplied `CF-Connecting-IP`; direct Worker and Service
Binding callers must be trusted. Do not substitute untrusted `X-Forwarded-For`.

The broker uses `CF-Connecting-IP` only for admission rate limiting, with a shared
`unknown` key when absent. A trusted binding caller can supply this header; the
binding does not authenticate it as an original client address. A compromised
caller can manipulate admission keys, but still needs a valid subject token and
an authorized request to obtain a token. The service-wide binding is not scoped
to one App; fixed App selection is enforced by the proxy code. The root runtime
already handles incoming assertions and outgoing tokens and must be trusted with
both.

Service Binding calls reach the Worker directly, so public-host routing and edge
controls must not be assumed to protect that hop. The broker's own admission,
OIDC authentication, and Token Issuance Policy remain mandatory. Local fixtures
and synthetic remote-binding probes establish header transport only. Production
verification must check the complete public ingress path and resistance to
client-supplied identity headers before claiming per-client admission behavior.

Configuration requirements belong in the service contract; validation ordering belongs in implementation documentation. Optional clarity improvement: replace the overlapping “Invalid receiver configuration” table row with “Missing or malformed GitHub App ID configuration.”

Documenting those exact values in the service contract is appropriate; renaming them would introduce unnecessary compatibility cost. The credential-exclusion rationale and present-tense wording are proportionate.

- **broker-response-utf8:** Preserves Token Exchange Client, issuer, broker, and OAuth field terminology. Implementation documentation is the established home for this internal library’s response validation. Optional tone refinement: replace the explanatory replacement-character sentence with direct behavior, such as “Malformed UTF-8 is rejected as an invalid response.” The existing wording is accurate, not a standards breach.

- **webhook-lifecycle-evidence:** Closed version-1 queue fields and extensible webhook payloads describe distinct, existing boundaries correctly. The service contract is the appropriate owner. The tests express publication and stable-processing guarantees without requiring a new production abstraction.

The independent changes remain semantically compatible with the supplied base and with one another: configuration validation precedes authentication, read failures map to rejection, publication remains awaited, logging changes preserve retry decisions, and malformed broker responses remain failures.

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/pr_spec_review
Payload:
One documentation correction and one evidence-label clarification; no runtime compatibility findings across the five heads.

1. **webhook-configuration — documentation scope:** `docs/service-contract.md:28–29,128` promises `500` for broadly “missing, malformed, or unreadable configuration” / “Invalid receiver configuration.” Only the App ID and webhook secret receive that validation. With an unavailable queue binding, a valid ping still returns `202`; a matching command reaches publication and returns `503` (`src/webhook.ts:74–88`). Narrow the prose and table to those two configuration values, preferably consolidating the overlapping `500` rows. This satisfies CONTRIBUTING’s requirement to “Resolve discrepancies among source, tests, and contracts.”

2. **webhook-lifecycle-evidence — evidence precision:** The test name at `test/worker.test.ts:66` and “job ownership guarantees” terminology suggest broader stability evidence than the assertions establish. The repository resource is already derived before the issuer wait (`src/github/reactions.ts:58–65`); the mutation experiment chiefly detects subsequent comment-ID drift. Describe the guarantee as preserving the validated reaction target while awaiting the issuer. The test need not prescribe deep-copying or prove general object immutability.

arguments.body:
## Summary

Reject missing or malformed GitHub App ID configuration and missing, empty, non-string, or unreadable Webhook Secrets before authentication. Valid direct Worker secrets and Secrets Store string results retain their existing behavior.

```text
validate GitHub App ID → resolve and validate Webhook Secret → authenticate delivery
```

The service contract identifies these configuration failures as `500`; queue write failures remain `503`. Implementation documentation describes the validation order.

## Evidence

- Initial regression verification: 11 added configuration cases failed against the original implementation, including a missing target matching a null App ID and non-string secret coercion. All 33 receiver acceptance tests passed after the fix with unchanged expectations.
- On base `94d6424c`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm run check`, and `pnpm run test:coverage` passed on Node 24.18.0 / pnpm 12.14.0: 298 tests across five projects, including real and built Worker tests and all three deployment dry runs. Final prose adjustments passed the pinned formatter and `git diff --check`.
- Standards and requirements reviewers inspected the complete changes and revised terminology/documentation; no actionable findings remain. The runtime code retains its original adversarial review. Reviewers did not rerun tests. Live production services and bindings were not exercised.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

Invalid GitHub App ID and Webhook Secret configuration now returns 500 before delivery authentication. No data migration or credential rotation is required.

**Blast Radius:** receiver

arguments.title: fix(token-exchange): reject malformed UTF-8 responses
arguments.body:
## Summary

Reject malformed UTF-8 in broker responses before the Token Exchange Client parses JSON.

```text
bounded response bytes → strict UTF-8 decoding → JSON parsing → consumed-field validation
```

Malformed success responses fail token acquisition. Malformed error responses retain their HTTP status and use `invalid_response`. Preserve response limits, token profile checks, scope behavior, and unconsumed extension fields. The service contract owns these outcomes; implementation documentation describes the decoding sequence and links to it.

## Evidence

- Initial regression verification: two added cases accepted replacement characters as a token or OAuth error code before the fix. Afterward, all 28 focused tests passed with unchanged expectations, including malformed-response rejection and extension-field compatibility.
- On base `94d6424c`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm run check`, and `pnpm run test:coverage` passed on Node 24.18.0 / pnpm 12.14.0: 290 tests across five projects, including real and built Worker tests and all three deployment dry runs. Final prose adjustments passed the pinned formatter and `git diff --check`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

Malformed broker responses fail token acquisition and cause valid Webhook Jobs to retry. Valid UTF-8 response behavior and token authority are unchanged; no credential rotation is required.

Invalid GitHub App ID and Webhook Secret configuration now returns 500 before delivery authentication. No data migration or credential rotation is required.

## Summary

Reject malformed UTF-8 in broker responses before the Token Exchange Client parses JSON.

```text
bounded response bytes → strict UTF-8 decoding → JSON parsing → consumed-field validation
```

Malformed success responses fail token acquisition. Malformed error responses retain their HTTP status and use `invalid_response`. Preserve response limits, token profile checks, scope behavior, and unconsumed extension fields. The service contract owns these outcomes; implementation documentation describes the decoding sequence and links to it.

## Evidence

- Initial regression verification: two added cases accepted replacement characters as a token or OAuth error code before the fix. Afterward, all 28 focused tests passed with unchanged expectations, including malformed-response rejection and extension-field compatibility.

## Summary

Return `400` problem details when the Webhook Receiver cannot read a request body, without exposing the stream exception or publishing a Webhook Job.

```text
request read failure → 400
request exceeds size limit → 413
```

The request-body adapter handles the failure; the shared response-body reader keeps its existing behavior. The service contract names the literal `Content-Length` header and distinguishes malformed lengths from unreadable bodies.

# Repository agent guidance

## Workflow

1. **Ground the task.** Inspect the worktree, affected source and tests, and the references triggered below in proportion to the task. Establish the requested outcome, governing contracts, and overlapping modifications before editing; preserve unrelated tracked and untracked work.
2. **Complete the requested work.** Resolve routine choices from repository evidence and carry prior agreement forward while its assumptions remain valid. Ask when unresolved requirements materially affect public contracts, compatibility, recovery, scope, or authorization; continue work that does not depend on the answer. For implementation, establish the intended behavior from the request and governing contracts, then align code, tests, and owned documentation with it. For reviews and plans, deliver analysis without unrequested implementation.
3. **Verify and review.** Follow [validation scope](CONTRIBUTING.md#validation-scope), then review the whole diff against the requested outcomes and affected failure paths. For implementation, resolve actionable in-scope findings and rerun affected checks. For reviews, support findings with triggers, consequences, and evidence; distinguish defects, unmet outcomes, unresolved contract questions, and optional improvements.
4. **Hand off with evidence.** Report each requested outcome, checks performed, and verification limits. Distinguish finished implementation from completed verification and readiness under the applicable contribution or release gates. If genuinely blocked, identify remaining work, the blocker, reasonable safe alternatives attempted, and the input or access needed. Commit, push, publish, or deploy only within the user's authorization.

## Design and contracts

- Choose the simplest cohesive design for the affected concern, including callers and lifecycle transitions. Preserve required behavior, public contracts, and lifecycle guarantees; distinguish these from existing implementation choices. Weigh concrete benefits against migration, regression, review, and maintenance costs.
- Preserve established domain, API, and protocol terminology. For terminology or trust-boundary changes, read [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md); rename internal symbols only for a concrete correctness or comprehension benefit.
- Extract helpers when they expose a coherent operation or lifecycle boundary, remove meaningful duplication, or clarify callers. A test seam needs behavioral evidence that justifies its interface and maintenance costs. For package boundaries, Worker entrypoints, bindings, or runtime changes, read [Implementation](docs/implementation.md).
- Before adding defenses or removing safeguards, identify the reachable failure scenario and required guarantees, compare simpler alternatives, and explain consequential tradeoffs and maintenance costs. A credible, consequential failure can justify an in-scope safeguard without a prior incident or known probability; uncertainty alone neither justifies nor disqualifies it. Where later trust or lifecycle decisions depend on validated values remaining stable, preserve them for that interval using the simplest adequate mechanism, such as ownership, encapsulation, copying, or immutability.
- For HTTP behavior, webhook acceptance, job classification, queue acknowledgement or retry changes, read the affected [service contract](docs/service-contract.md) sections. For authentication, external input, token exchange, permissions, or logging changes, read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md); for issuer or broker binding changes, also read [runtime bindings](docs/implementation.md#runtime-bindings). Validate consumed external values at their owning trust boundary, including newly crossed boundaries; TypeScript types alone do not establish trust. Apply closed-field validation only where the contract requires it.
- For routing, Wrangler configuration, deployment automation, or artifacts, read [Deployment](docs/deployment.md). Keep source-owned defaults separate from production configuration; the root Wrangler configuration is a test harness. Local fixtures and dry runs do not by themselves verify live service configuration or end-to-end production behavior.
- Use the pinned runtime, package manager, scripts, and generators. Keep dependency, formatting, and generated changes necessary to the concern. Regenerate affected environment declarations from Wrangler configuration rather than hand-editing them.

## Evidence and documentation

- Ground implementation claims in source or direct experiments and external compatibility claims in primary sources or direct experiments. State what was and was not verified.
- Choose independent behavioral evidence at the affected boundary, including rejection, retry, and acknowledgement paths. When consolidating tests, account for retained guarantees and justify consequential coverage removed. To claim a regression test detects a defect, observe it fail against faulty behavior with unchanged expectations and pass after the fix.
- For documentation changes, follow [documentation ownership](CONTRIBUTING.md#documentation-ownership). Keep each fact and policy authoritative in one place, with explicit task-triggered pointers. Keep evaluation history and completed plans with their change records. Repository guidance must remain usable without personal agent configuration.
# Contributing

Keep changes cohesive, explicit, and grounded in the service contract.
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) owns repository agent guidance; this document owns
validation scope and contribution requirements. Personal agent configuration
is not a prerequisite. Tool versions and command definitions remain
authoritative in `package.json`, `.nvmrc`, and the lockfile. For dependency
setup and updates, follow [dependency tooling](#dependency-tooling).

## Validation scope

Use focused checks during implementation. Before declaring a change fully
verified or ready, or opening or updating a pull request, apply the matching gate:

- **Agent instructions or prose only:** review consistency, local links, and the
  final diff; run `pnpm exec oxfmt --check <changed-markdown-files>` with the
  pinned formatter and `git diff --check`. For instruction changes, walk through
  representative triggering, safe, and unrelated tasks. Label these as static
  walkthroughs unless actual agent trials were observed. Static walkthroughs
  suffice for straightforward instruction corrections. Use observed agent trials
  to resolve material disagreements about agent behavior and before claiming
  that wording improves behavior; limit claims to what the trials establish.
  A full install and application suite are not required solely for prose changes.
- **Code, configuration, dependencies, generated artifacts, or executable
  examples:** establish dependencies with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and
  use Node 24 and the pinned pnpm to run the full `pnpm run check` and
  `pnpm run test:coverage`, plus focused checks that establish the changed behavior. A previously verified frozen installation may be reused while its
  dependency inputs remain unchanged. Focused checks do not replace the full
  final check. The aggregate check includes Worker deployment dry runs; it does
  not deploy.

For runtime behavior or binding configuration changes, cover the affected unit and real Worker
entrypoint projects described in [Tests and validation](docs/implementation.md#tests-and-validation).
For changes to authentication, token exchange, permissions, queue processing, or logging
behavior, verify affected success and failure paths against [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md)
and the [service contract](docs/service-contract.md). After implementing such
changes, perform a distinct adversarial review of the affected trust and
lifecycle boundaries, with depth proportionate to the changed guarantees.
The implementing agent may perform this pass for smaller changes. Consequential
changes to who can obtain authority, what can trigger external effects, or
whether accepted work can be lost require an independent reviewer.

A separate agent, even using the same model, qualifies when it assesses the
requirements, final diff, relevant source, and tests without being led by the
implementer's conclusions. Report the review's actual scope and limitations;
this provides a separate assessment, not model diversity or human approval.
Resolve actionable in-scope findings and rerun affected checks before readiness.
If required independent review is unavailable, complete other authorized work
and report verification as incomplete, identifying the missing review and what
would satisfy it. Self-review does not substitute for that gate.

Once appropriate checks pass, broaden or repeat them only for new changes,
failures, or unresolved concerns. Report exact commands and distinguish passed,
failed, and unrun checks. Separate environmental failures from source defects;
try reasonable safe scoped alternatives. An unavailable required check leaves
verification incomplete even if implementation is finished; report the missing
check and what would allow it to run.
Local checks do not establish remote CI success or waive required CI checks.

For deployment changes, follow [Deployment](docs/deployment.md), including the
separate deployment repository's validation. Publishing or releasing still
requires the [source publishing requirements](#source-publishing), including
the full check and coverage gates.

## Documentation ownership

Before handoff, update the authoritative document for each affected concern:

- [Service contract](docs/service-contract.md) for externally observable behavior.
- [Implementation](docs/implementation.md) for package layout, Worker entrypoints, request flow, bindings, and test boundaries.
- [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) for source/deployment ownership and this document for publish-readiness checks.
- [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md) for terminology and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for security policy.

Resolve discrepancies among source, tests, and contracts before encoding new
guidance. Use present-tense documentation for implemented behavior.

## Public source boundary

Do not commit local deployment state or secrets. In particular, keep `.dev.vars`, `.env`, `.wrangler/`, `.local-secrets/`, Cloudflare tokens, and webhook secrets out of commits.

## Source publishing

Use Node 24 and the pinned pnpm to run `pnpm run check` and
`pnpm run test:coverage` before publishing source artifacts.

Before publishing source artifacts, review `git status --short` and ignored local
files. Build artifacts from tracked source only; exclude dependency directories,
local deployment state, and secrets. Confirm generated environment types cover
all three Workers and binding names match the source/deployment configuration.
See [deployment requirements](docs/deployment.md) for production authorization,
queue recovery, and coordinated Token Endpoint verification.

Repository maintainers keep secret scanning and push protection, Dependabot
security updates, and private vulnerability reporting (where available) enabled.
The protected branch requires the aggregate `ci` check.

## Dependency tooling

Use Node 24 and the exact pnpm version in `packageManager`. Install it from the
repository root, then verify it before installing dependencies. When migrating
an existing Corepack installation, run `corepack disable pnpm` once first to
remove its pnpm shims.

```bash
npm install --global "$(node -p 'require("./package.json").packageManager')"
node --run pnpm:check
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

CI installs the manifest pin with `pnpm/action-setup`. The local `check` command
retains the version guard for developer environments. `pmOnFail: ignore` keeps
the lockfile as one YAML document for GitHub's dependency graph; direct pnpm commands do not automatically select or enforce the
pin. Adding config dependencies requires reviewing that compatibility assumption.

Dependency updates permit intermediate peer conflicts while grouped updates are
assembled. `autoInstallPeers: false` keeps required peers explicit. The
`peer-dependencies:check` command runs `pnpm peers check` without changing the
lockfile; a frozen install alone does not perform this check. `dedupe:check` rejects avoidable lockfile duplication. Both checks run in
`check` and the required CI dependency job, alongside frozen manifest/lockfile
validation. CI also rejects any lockfile changes produced by validation.

The scheduled `pnpm-up` workflow updates pnpm to the latest stable release,
including new majors, using the same release-age policy. The step explicitly
forwards that policy because `self-update` ignores project release-age settings.
It overrides `pmOnFail` for this command so the manifest pin is updated. A changed
`packageManager` pin is committed before dependencies are updated with that
version; unchanged pins do not create empty commits.

`autoDedupe` consolidates compatible resolutions during updates, including across
workspace projects outside a command's filter. Frozen installs leave the graph
unchanged; `lockfile.includeResolutionSettings` records the selected deduplication
and linking settings.
`verifyDepsBeforeRun: error` stops pnpm scripts when dependencies are stale; it
does not guard `node --run`, so install explicitly before validation.

Dependency resolution uses a three-day release age, aligned with npm Dependabot
cooldown where configured. Frozen installs also verify lockfile supply-chain
policy. Dependency build scripts require explicit `allowBuilds` decisions;
`strictDepBuilds` rejects unreviewed builds.

# Repository agent guidance

## Workflow

1. **Ground the task.** Inspect the worktree, affected source and tests, and the references triggered below in proportion to the task. Establish the requested outcome, governing contracts, and overlapping modifications before editing; preserve unrelated tracked and untracked work.
2. **Complete the requested work.** Resolve routine choices from repository evidence and carry prior agreement forward while its assumptions remain valid. Ask when unresolved requirements materially affect public contracts, compatibility, recovery, scope, or authorization; continue work that does not depend on the answer. For implementation, establish the intended behavior from the request and governing contracts, then align code, tests, and owned documentation with it. For reviews and plans, deliver analysis without unrequested implementation.
3. **Verify and review.** Follow [validation scope](CONTRIBUTING.md#validation-scope), then review the whole diff against the requested outcomes and affected failure paths. For implementation, resolve actionable in-scope findings and rerun affected checks. For reviews, support findings with triggers, consequences, and evidence; distinguish defects, unmet outcomes, unresolved contract questions, and optional improvements.
4. **Hand off with evidence.** Report each requested outcome, checks performed, and verification limits. Distinguish finished implementation from completed verification and readiness under the applicable contribution or release gates. If genuinely blocked, identify remaining work, the blocker, reasonable safe alternatives attempted, and the input or access needed. ## Design and contracts

- Choose the simplest cohesive design for the affected concern, including callers and lifecycle transitions. Preserve required behavior, public contracts, and lifecycle guarantees; distinguish these from existing implementation choices. Weigh concrete benefits against migration, regression, review, and maintenance costs.
- Preserve established domain, API, and protocol terminology. For terminology or trust-boundary changes, read [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md); rename internal symbols only for a concrete correctness or comprehension benefit.
- Extract helpers when they expose a coherent operation or lifecycle boundary, remove meaningful duplication, or clarify callers. A test seam needs behavioral evidence that justifies its interface and maintenance costs. For package boundaries, Worker entrypoints, bindings, or runtime changes, read [Implementation](docs/implementation.md).
- Before adding defenses or removing safeguards, identify the reachable failure scenario and required guarantees, compare simpler alternatives, and explain consequential tradeoffs and maintenance costs. A credible, consequential failure can justify an in-scope safeguard without a prior incident or known probability; uncertainty alone neither justifies nor disqualifies it. Where later trust or lifecycle decisions depend on validated values remaining stable, preserve them for that interval using the simplest adequate mechanism, such as ownership, encapsulation, copying, or immutability.
- For HTTP behavior, webhook acceptance, job classification, queue acknowledgement or retry changes, read the affected [service contract](docs/service-contract.md) sections. For authentication, external input, token exchange, permissions, or logging changes, read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md); for issuer or broker binding changes, also read [runtime bindings](docs/implementation.md#runtime-bindings). Keep changes cohesive, explicit, and grounded in the service contract.
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) owns repository agent guidance; this document owns
validation scope and contribution requirements. Personal agent configuration
is not a prerequisite. Tool versions and command definitions remain
authoritative in `package.json`, `.nvmrc`, and the lockfile. For dependency
setup and updates, follow [dependency tooling](#dependency-tooling).

`pnpm run test:coverage` before publishing source artifacts.

CI installs the manifest pin with `pnpm/action-setup`. The local `check` command
retains the version guard for developer environments. `pmOnFail: ignore` keeps
the lockfile as one YAML document for GitHub's dependency graph; direct pnpm commands do not automatically select or enforce the
pin. Adding config dependencies requires reviewing that compatibility assumption.

Dependency updates permit intermediate peer conflicts while grouped updates are
assembled. `autoInstallPeers: false` keeps required peers explicit. The
`peer-dependencies:check` command runs `pnpm peers check` without changing the
lockfile; a frozen install alone does not perform this check. `dedupe:check` rejects avoidable lockfile duplication. Both checks run in
`check` and the required CI dependency job, alongside frozen manifest/lockfile
validation. CI also rejects any lockfile changes produced by validation.

unchanged; `lockfile.includeResolutionSettings` records the selected deduplication
and linking settings.
`verifyDepsBeforeRun: error` stops pnpm scripts when dependencies are stale; it
does not guard `node --run`, so install explicitly before validation.

Dependency resolution uses a three-day release age, aligned with npm Dependabot
cooldown where configured. Frozen installs also verify lockfile supply-chain
policy. Dependency build scripts require explicit `allowBuilds` decisions;

# Deployment

This repository contains the public source, tests, and public-safe Wrangler templates for the cyspbot root page, Token Endpoint Proxy, GitHub webhook receiver, and GitHub webhook processor. It does not contain production domains, routes, Cloudflare resource identifiers, or secret values.

## Deployable Workers

`@cyspbot/cyspbot` deploys Worker `cyspbot` as the Custom Domain origin for the root page and Token Endpoint Proxy. Its [service contract](service-contract.md#routes) owns request matching and responses.

`@cyspbot/github-webhook-receiver` deploys Worker `cyspbot-github-webhook-receiver` for `POST /github/webhooks`.

`@cyspbot/github-webhook-processor` deploys Worker `cyspbot-github-webhook-processor` as the consumer for the status-reaction job queue.

The source-owned Worker configurations define their entrypoints, compatibility dates and flags, required binding names, safe local/dry-run service targets, and safe local values for the root proxy and processor's token-client variables. Production deployment configuration replaces those targets and supplies the deployment-owned endpoint values, audience, and issuer properties.

## Separate deployment pipeline

[`chikachow/cyspbot-deploy`](https://github.com/chikachow/cyspbot-deploy) pins this repository as a submodule and owns production Worker code, bindings, variables, validation, deployment workflows, and smoke probes. [`chikachow/infrastructure`](https://github.com/chikachow/infrastructure) manages the queues, retention, queue consumer, Custom Domain, and routes with Terraform. The webhook Route selects the receiver, and the retained Token Endpoint Route selects the cyspbot Worker. A cyspbot source update must pass its own checks and strict Wrangler dry runs in the deployment repository before deployment.

The source workflow `.github/workflows/run-cyspbot-deploy-update.yml` is responsible for dispatching the deployment repository's source-update workflow after successful `main` CI. It obtains a short-lived GitHub token through `cyspbot-app-token-action`.

The production deployment configuration retains the root Worker's broker HTTP
Service Binding, the receiver's queue producer binding, and the processor's
WorkloadIdentityIssuer RPC and broker Service Bindings. Terraform owns the processor's queue consumer attachment and its
retry and dead-letter settings. The source Wrangler consumer declaration is
for local tests and dry runs; production overlays omit consumers and routes.
The deployment configuration supplies the logical Workload Identity Token
audience and broker Token Endpoint URL as
separate variables. The issuer binding supplies the `WorkloadIdentityIssuer`
RPC together with its `subject` and `allowedAudiences` properties, while the
broker binding supplies the broker transport. The broker verifies the workload
identity assertion and performs authorization at its Token Endpoint.

## Delivery recovery

The deployment operator owns recovery of failed webhook deliveries and exhausted queue jobs. GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed webhooks; this source does not run a delivery-recovery scheduler. Queue durability starts only after the receiver successfully publishes the job.

After resolving an ingress failure, inspect the GitHub App's recent webhook deliveries and manually redeliver the failed delivery. See [GitHub's redelivery procedure](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/testing-and-troubleshooting-webhooks/redelivering-webhooks).

Every failed valid job retries and reaches `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq` if
it exhausts the queue's retry budget. Inspect the DLQ and bounded processor
diagnostics, resolve the cause, then choose which jobs to replay through the
primary queue or deliberately discard. Replay requests credentials again and
does not bypass authorization. There is no job-age cutoff or automatic DLQ
replay. Invalid queue jobs are rejected before token acquisition and are not
retained for replay.

For manual replay, publish the unchanged job body to the primary queue and
confirm publication before acknowledging the DLQ copy. If publication or
acknowledgement has an ambiguous outcome, a duplicate is possible; repeating
the same reaction under the same GitHub App identity is safe. Do not purge a
DLQ job before its replay is durably published.

Monitor the DLQ backlog for recovery work. A `github_webhook_job_retrying` log
records a retry request, not confirmation of a DLQ transfer, including on the
last attempt. Unconsumed DLQ messages expire when their retention period ends.

Primary-queue retention also limits recovery: a job can expire before exhausting
its retries when delivery is delayed or consumers are unavailable. DLQ retention
does not extend that primary-queue window. Verify both retention settings against
the intended recovery window; this policy does not guarantee indefinite delivery.

The operator inspects the DLQ at least every 24 hours. Automated alerts are
currently unconfigured; recovery does not depend on email notification. Queue
retention is managed in Terraform, not by the Worker deployment pipeline.

Broker policy must authorize the processor's workload identity for the intended repositories and the exact requested scope, `issues:write pull_requests:write`. Keep both permissions until issue and pull-request conversation-comment behavior has been verified against the deployed GitHub App and broker policy.

## Local validation only

This repository's deployment command is a dry run:

```bash
fnm exec --using=24 pnpm run deploy:dry-run
```

Do not add production credentials, domains, or routes to this repository.

## Token Endpoint Proxy prerequisites

The cyspbot Worker's Token Endpoint Proxy requires a canonical HTTPS Token Endpoint
variable and a `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER` HTTP Service Binding to the broker's
default handler. The binding selects the Worker; the URL selects its App path.
Deploy source and binding configuration together. An arbitrary public HTTPS
broker target is not supported by this proxy transport, and there is no public
fetch fallback. The broker's public canonical endpoint remains available to
its direct clients. Do not add an issuer binding or a named RPC entrypoint to
the root Worker for forwarding.

Verify the complete public ingress path preserves the original client's
`CF-Connecting-IP` and replaces spoofed client identity headers. The broker owns
admission with a shared `unknown` bucket for missing identity. Local fixtures and
synthetic remote-binding probes cannot establish edge identity authenticity.
See `SECURITY.md` for the trust boundary and public-ingress control limitations.

Terraform manages the production Custom Domains and Routes separately from
Worker publication. The retained vanity Token Endpoint Route selects the cyspbot
Worker. The [deployment repository](https://github.com/chikachow/cyspbot-deploy#token-endpoint-verification)
owns production verification of binding reachability, canonical and vanity OAuth
responses, edge admission identity, and the webhook-to-reaction flow.

# cyspbot deployment pipeline

This private repository deploys the `chikachow/cyspbot` root page, Token Endpoint Proxy, GitHub
webhook receiver, and GitHub webhook processor to production. The `cyspbot`
Worker owns the root page and `/token` convenience forwarding through its broker HTTP Service Binding. The separate
`chikachow/github-app-token-broker-deploy` pipeline publishes the canonical broker
App endpoint. Terraform manages the Custom Domains and webhook route.

The source implementation is pinned as the `src/cyspbot` git submodule. This
repository owns the production Wrangler configuration overlays, Cloudflare
resource identifiers and GitHub Actions deployment workflows.
[Infrastructure](https://github.com/chikachow/infrastructure) manages the queues,
queue consumer, Custom Domain and routes.

## Source

`src/cyspbot` pins the source commit that is eligible for production
deployment. Updating that submodule updates the source revision this repository
builds, checks, dry-runs, and deploys. The normal updater selects source `main`. This repository does not impose
an additional source-ancestry gate.

Install the [pinned pnpm version](#dependency-tooling) first.

```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
node --run source:install
node --run check
node --run source:check
node --run deploy:dry-run
```

See [dependency tooling](#dependency-tooling) for the dependency update policy
and validation gates.

`node --run knip` checks deployment-owned scripts, dependencies and exports as
part of `check` and the single CI job. `knip.jsonc` lists the deployment CLI and
actual Node test pattern so unused helper files and exports are reported.
Wrangler runs from the separately checked source submodule and is therefore
excluded from the deployment binary dependency report.

## Workers

The three deployed Workers are listed in
`scripts/deploy-configuration.mjs`. Production bindings, variables, and Cloudflare resource identifiers live in
`config/workers/*.wrangler.jsonc`.

Worker `cyspbot` serves the `cyspbot.chikachow.org` Custom Domain as its
origin for the root page and `/token`. The more specific `/github/webhooks*`
Worker Route executes first and selects the webhook receiver.

Each Worker config filename must match the Worker name:
`config/workers/<worker-name>.wrangler.jsonc`.

The processor uses broker and `WorkloadIdentityIssuer` Service Bindings configured
in its production overlay. The root Worker uses a broker HTTP Service Binding without an issuer binding.
The broker still verifies subject tokens and applies its issuance policy; transport
reachability grants no token-issuance permission. The binding selects the broker
Worker, while the canonical endpoint URL selects its App path. Trusted binding
callers can supply admission identity headers; public callers must receive
edge-established identity at cyspbot ingress. The internal hop does not traverse
the broker hostname's public ingress controls. See the source [Token Exchange Client](https://github.com/chikachow/cyspbot/blob/main/docs/implementation.md#token-exchange-client)
for the protocol contract.

The deployment script runs a strict Wrangler dry-run for every configured Worker
before a production deploy. `node --run deploy:dry-run` stops after the dry-runs.
`node --run deploy` runs the dry-runs first, then deploys every Worker with
Wrangler strict checks enabled.

## Cloudflare Configuration

The production Wrangler overlays bind existing Cloudflare resources. Keep those
values in `config/workers/*.wrangler.jsonc`, not duplicated in documentation.
Worker secret values are supplied by Cloudflare Secrets Store; do not add secret
values to the Wrangler overlays.

## Local Deployment

Authenticate Wrangler locally:

```bash
node scripts/source-pnpm.mjs exec wrangler login
```

For non-interactive deployments, provide the Cloudflare credentials consumed by
Wrangler. The deploy scripts run Node with `--env-file-if-exists=.env`, and
explicit environment variables take precedence over `.env` values.

```bash
node --run source:install
node --run deploy:dry-run
node --run deploy
```

## GitHub Actions

CI is orchestrated by `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Its single `ci` job installs
frozen source dependencies, runs the full `source:check`, installs frozen private
dependencies, runs `check` including the private Node configuration tests, and
dry-runs every production Worker. Every step must succeed.

Production deployment runs from `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` after a
successful `ci` workflow on `main`. The workflow owns its required secrets,
stale-main guard, deployment command, and root, fallback, and webhook
post-deploy probes.

## Token Endpoint verification

The root overlay's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER` binding selects the broker Worker
and `TOKEN_PROXY_ENDPOINT` supplies its canonical App endpoint URL;
the processor overlay's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER_TOKEN_ENDPOINT` selects the
endpoint reached through its broker Service Binding.

Terraform retains the vanity `/token*` Route targeting `cyspbot`. Worker
publication does not provision queues, attach consumers, or change routes.

For changes affecting token delivery, verify the deployed source pin, endpoint
configuration and Service Bindings together. Check canonical and vanity OAuth
responses, least-privilege issuance and action callers, and preservation of
edge-established client identity despite spoofed forwarding headers. Local
forwarding tests and credential-free probes do not establish those properties.
Before changing transport, review any dependency on the broker hostname's
public ingress controls; HTTP Service Bindings bypass them.

Verify webhook delivery through the queue and processor to the expected GitHub
reaction when changing that flow. Use the source's
[delivery recovery procedure](https://github.com/chikachow/cyspbot/blob/main/docs/deployment.md#delivery-recovery)
for failed deliveries and exhausted jobs. Never purge jobs as part of a deployment.
Check for pending runs that could republish an incompatible version. Failed
publication or probes require operator diagnosis; they do not undo published
Workers or Terraform changes.

## Dependency tooling

Use Node 24 and the exact pnpm version in `packageManager`. Install it from the
repository root, then verify it before installing dependencies. When migrating
an existing Corepack installation, run `corepack disable pnpm` once first to
remove its pnpm shims.

```bash
npm install --global "$(node -p 'require("./package.json").packageManager')"
node --run pnpm:check
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

CI installs the manifest pin with `pnpm/action-setup`. The local `check` command
retains the version guard for developer environments. `pmOnFail: ignore` keeps
the lockfile as one YAML document for GitHub's dependency graph; direct pnpm commands do not automatically select or enforce the
pin. Adding config dependencies requires reviewing that compatibility assumption.

`check` validates the deployment-owned manifest and lockfile, strictly checks
peer requirements with `pnpm peers check`, and rejects avoidable lockfile
duplication. The single CI job runs these checks once and rejects lockfile changes. The full
`source:check` separately validates the pinned source tree.
Peer validation reads the lockfile; deduplication checks disable lifecycle scripts. Ordinary
resolution permits intermediate peer conflicts, while `autoInstallPeers: false`
keeps required peers explicit.

`autoDedupe` consolidates compatible resolutions during updates, including across
workspace projects outside a command's filter. Frozen installs leave the graph
unchanged; `lockfile.includeResolutionSettings` records the selected deduplication
and linking settings.
`verifyDepsBeforeRun: error` stops pnpm scripts when dependencies are stale; it
does not guard `node --run`, so install explicitly before validation.

Dependency resolution uses a three-day release age, aligned with npm Dependabot
cooldown where configured. Frozen installs also verify lockfile supply-chain
policy. Dependency build scripts require explicit `allowBuilds` decisions;
`strictDepBuilds` rejects unreviewed builds.

The source submodule keeps its own toolchain pin. `scripts/source-pnpm.mjs` reads
that pin and invokes `pnpm with <version>` from the source directory. This also
selects the version for nested pnpm commands, so deployment and source upgrades
can merge independently. Use the launcher for source commands; an outer
`pnpm -C` invocation does not select the source pin.

## Consolidated CI

The single `ci` job runs the full source checks, all deployment-local checks and
production dry-runs. Source and private dependencies retain their own pinned pnpm
versions and frozen lockfiles. Source validation runs locally on every CI run.
The final guard rejects tracked changes against `HEAD`, including staged changes,
and rejects untracked or modified source files.

Sharing one runner saves repeated setup and per-job minute rounding, at the cost
of serial feedback and a larger rerun unit. Production deployment remains in its
separate workflow with its existing exact-revision checkout, freshness checks,
production environment, credentials and live probes.
